title: Hide Artifacts: Bind Mounts
summary: Bind Mounts abuse a Linux feature that maps a directory or file onto another location in the same file system. An adversary with root privileges can overlay the process directory of a benign process onto the process directory belonging to a malicious one. Utilities such as ps and top read process information through the file system, so the kernel follows the mount and reports the benign details instead of the real ones. The malicious process continues to run while its visible metadata, its executable link and other artefacts appear to belong to something trusted. Detection rests on the mount table, on privileged mount activity in audit records, and on comparisons between raw process accounting and what user space tools display.

beginner.definition: Linux keeps information about every running program in a special folder. Tools that list programs read from that folder. A bind mount is a feature that makes one folder appear in another place. An attacker with full rights can point the folder of a harmless program over the folder of their harmful one. The listing tools then show the harmless program.
beginner.whyItMatters: If your process list is wrong, your investigation starts in the wrong place. The malicious program may stay invisible while you study a harmless one. Other tools that read the same folders can be fooled in the same way. This behaviour needs high privileges, but those are exactly what an attacker works to obtain. Comparing different sources of process data is therefore important.
howItWorks: Linux stores details about each running program in a folder under the proc directory.
Listing tools such as ps and top read those folders to build their output.
A bind mount makes the contents of one folder appear at another location.
An attacker with root rights mounts a harmless program's folder over their own program's folder.
The listing tools follow the mount and show the harmless program's details instead.
The malicious program keeps running, but its visible record now points at something trusted.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats with a name plate beside every door. The building manager checks the plates to know who lives where. One resident unscrews their own plate and fixes a neighbour's plate over it. Now the corridor shows two doors belonging to the same trusted neighbour. The manager walks past and sees nothing unusual, because both plates match. A bind mount is that swapped plate. The person is still inside the flat, but the label on the door tells a different story.
takeaways: A bind mount can make one folder appear somewhere else and hide the original.
Process listing tools can report innocent details for a hidden program.
Mount activity started by a privileged account is worth reviewing.

objectives: Explain what a bind mount does to the layout of a file system.
Describe how Linux exposes process information through the file system.
Explain why listing tools can show misleading details about a process.
Identify the records that capture mount changes and privileged activity.
Suggest a way to corroborate process data using a second source.
